title: Family catering Dubai: make sharing easy
focus: Choose dishes that can be passed and served comfortably in your dining space. A family-style meal should offer enough variety for different preferences while keeping the selection coherent. Tell us about children, older guests and essential dietary requirements so portions and service can be considered together. Confirm how the published guest range applies to your group and which changes need a revised quote. The aim is a relaxed meal where the host can spend time at the table.

sections.title: Give the menu a clear direction
paragraphs: Begin with a few dishes or flavours that your guests will enjoy, then build a balanced selection around them. A strong menu includes variety in texture, colour and richness without trying to cover every possible preference with a separate dish. The most useful question is how the food will work as a complete meal or reception.

Consider the time of day and the length of service. A short welcome reception needs a different amount and style of food from an evening where canapés replace dinner. Similarly, a working lunch should be easy to serve and enjoy within the available break.

Menu examples are a starting point for discussion. Ingredients, dietary variations and the practical requirements of your venue need to be reviewed before the final selection is confirmed. That gives the team room to recommend food that suits the occasion and can be served well.

sections.title: Plan quantities around the format, not just the headcount
paragraphs: A guest count becomes useful when it is connected to the way people will eat. A short reception with light bites needs a different food plan from an evening where passed dishes are the main meal. Children, late arrivals and guests attending only part of an event may also affect the quantities required.

Tell us whether other food will be available and whether the service follows a meal earlier in the day. The chef can then recommend a sensible balance of dishes and portions. Generosity should mean guests can enjoy the occasion comfortably, rather than simply ordering more of every item.

Confirm the final numbers by the deadline in your proposal. A late increase may affect ingredients, equipment and staff as well as food quantity. Clear updates allow the team to assess the change properly and confirm any effect on the price or service plan.

sections.title: Give every guest a considered option
paragraphs: Collect dietary requirements before the final menu is agreed. Record how many guests each requirement applies to and distinguish preferences from allergies or other essential restrictions. A clear list helps the culinary team assess suitable dishes and the preparation arrangements they would need.

A vegetarian or vegan choice should feel like a complete part of the menu. Consider its portion, accompaniments and presentation alongside the other dishes, rather than removing an ingredient and assuming the result will be satisfying. Sauces, garnishes, breads and desserts also need attention.

Allergy requests require a specific discussion of ingredients and kitchen conditions. Labels and separate serving utensils can support a plan, but they do not by themselves guarantee the absence of cross-contact. Share the details early so the team can assess the request honestly and confirm what can be accommodated before you book.

sections.title: Choose the support that makes hosting easier
paragraphs: Decide who will do the work after the food arrives. If your own team will lay out platters, replenish drinks and clear the space, a delivery arrangement may be suitable. If you want to stay with your guests, discuss setup, service staff, equipment and clear-down as part of the proposal.

Different formats create different demands. A buffet needs attention to presentation and replenishment; a plated meal requires coordination between the kitchen and table; passed food needs staff who can circulate comfortably through the room. The number of guests matters, but so do the layout and pace of service.

Ask for included roles and hours to be clearly identified. Additional items such as table linen, crockery, glassware, bar support or styling should be confirmed explicitly. A well-defined scope lets you understand the service you are buying and helps the team prepare for the work you expect.

sections.title: A clear brief gives the menu a better starting point
paragraphs: Start with the date, venue and number of guests, then describe how you want the occasion to feel. A working lunch, an evening reception and a family celebration need different menus and service rhythms. Tell us when people will eat, whether they will be seated or standing and which parts of the event you would like myCHEF to handle.

Include essential dietary requirements and the facilities available at the venue. A brief does not need to be long, but it should distinguish what is essential from what would simply be nice to have. If you have a spending range, share it alongside the scope so the proposal can prioritise the right elements.

We can then discuss a suitable format, food selection and staffing plan. Your written proposal brings those decisions together, giving you a clear reference for what is included before you confirm the booking.

sections.title: Compare the complete proposal
paragraphs: Read the price together with the menu and service scope. Two proposals can have different totals because one includes equipment, staffing or a longer service period that the other does not. Compare them against the same guest count and requirements before deciding which is the better fit.

Check the minimum order, included hours, delivery or transport arrangements and how applicable VAT is shown. If the menu uses a starting price, ask which choices could change it. Premium ingredients, additional stations, extended service and extra hospitality support may need separate pricing.

The written proposal should also explain the payment schedule and the terms for changes or cancellation. Use the terms attached to your booking, as a private occasion and a corporate contract may have different arrangements. A clear comparison gives you confidence in the decision and helps avoid assumptions about what a headline price includes.
